clinicalPearls: Characterised by excessive expiratory narrowing of the central airways due to weakness of the airway wall, causing dynamic collapse with cough, forced expiration, or Valsalva
Causes a harsh barking or seal-like cough, breathlessness, wheeze, difficulty clearing secretions, and recurrent infections
May be congenital (including association with tracheo-oesophageal anomalies) or acquired from prolonged intubation, chronic inflammation, COPD, trauma, or extrinsic compression
Excessive dynamic airway collapse describes bulging of the posterior membrane, distinct from cartilage-based malacia, though the two overlap clinically
Dynamic imaging or bronchoscopy is essential, as the collapse is seen during expiration or coughing and may be missed on static inspiratory studies
A common diagnostic threshold is more than about half expiratory reduction in luminal cross-section, ideally confirmed dynamically
Management ranges from treating underlying disease and positive-pressure support to airway stenting or surgical tracheobronchoplasty in severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: Tracheobronchomalacia results from structural weakness of the central airway wall, either from deficient or softened cartilaginous support or from laxity and redundancy of the posterior membranous wall. During expiration and coughing, when intrathoracic pressure rises above intraluminal pressure, the weakened airway collapses excessively, obstructing airflow and impairing the shear forces needed to clear secretions. Congenital forms reflect immature or deficient cartilage, while acquired forms follow injury from prolonged intubation or tracheostomy, chronic inflammation, recurrent infection, emphysema, trauma, or chronic compression by adjacent structures. The dynamic nature of the collapse explains why symptoms are provoked by exertion and cough and why static imaging can underestimate severity.
additionalDifferentials: Fixed central airway stenosis or tumour
Extrinsic airway compression (goitre, vascular ring, mediastinal mass)
additionalInvestigations: Dynamic expiratory CT of the airways to quantify collapse
Bronchoscopy with observation during forced expiration and coughing
Pulmonary function tests with flow-volume loops
Assessment for underlying causes such as prior intubation, COPD, or compression
Evaluation for tracheo-oesophageal anomalies in congenital cases
Trial of positive airway pressure to assess symptomatic and functional response
redFlags: Recurrent respiratory failure or life-threatening episodes of near-complete airway collapse
Severe secretion retention with recurrent pneumonia
Rapidly worsening symptoms suggesting an evolving compressive lesion
Syncope or exercise-limiting obstruction from severe dynamic collapse
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on severity and cause; mild disease is often managed conservatively with good quality of life, while severe symptomatic malacia can be disabling but may improve substantially with positive-pressure support, stenting, or tracheobronchoplasty.
pitfalls: Relying on static inspiratory imaging and missing the dynamic collapse
Mislabelling the disease as refractory asthma or COPD and escalating ineffective therapy
Overlooking a treatable underlying cause such as extrinsic compression
Proceeding to airway stenting without a trial confirming benefit, given stent-related complications
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Continuous positive airway pressure as a pneumatic stent to splint the central airways open during expiration and improve secretion clearance in symptomatic disease
Optimise airway clearance with cough-assist techniques, mucolytics and pulmonary rehabilitation to counter impaired secretion clearance
Treat contributing conditions including inhaled therapy for coexisting COPD and relief of extrinsic compression where present
Prompt culture-guided antibiotics for the recurrent lower respiratory infections driven by retained secretions
Short-term silicone airway stent trial to identify patients likely to benefit from surgery
Surgical tracheobronchoplasty to stabilise the posterior membranous wall in severe, disabling, well-selected disease
Manage in a multidisciplinary airway service spanning interventional pulmonology and thoracic surgery, reserving intervention for genuinely symptomatic collapse
